html:
Assyria was a kingdom in northern Mesopotamia, centred on the city of Assur on the Tigris, that grew into the largest empire the world had yet seen. The chart shows its Middle and Neo-Assyrian empires, from about 1365 BCE to its fall in 609 BCE. At its height around 670 BCE it ruled from Egypt to western Iran.

Assur was a trading city long before it was an empire; around 1900 BCE its merchants ran a trading colony at Kanesh in Anatolia. Around 1365 BCE King Ashur-uballit I broke free of the kingdom of Mitanni and made Assyria a great power. It survived the crisis at the end of the Bronze Age, and from about 911 BCE its kings set out to conquer again.

  • Tiglath-Pileser III (745 to 727 BCE) built a standing army and turned conquered lands into provinces run by governors.
  • Assyria moved whole peoples to break resistance. In 722 BCE it destroyed the kingdom of Israel and deported many of its people.
  • Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE and rebuilt Nineveh as a vast capital.
  • Esarhaddon conquered Egypt in 671 BCE.
  • Ashurbanipal sacked Susa and gathered a great library of clay tablets.

Assyrian rule was famous for its cruelty, which its own palace reliefs advertise. It was also very good at roads, records and taxes, and later empires copied its methods. After Ashurbanipal, civil war weakened it. The Babylonians and the Medes sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE, and the last Assyrian army was beaten in 609 BCE. Its lands passed to the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
